correctness.rationale: At a projective gradient zero, a zero coordinate would force every coordinate to vanish. In characteristic 2 the gradient is the cyclic list of squares; otherwise multiplying the nonzero-coordinate gradient equations forces 33=0. In characteristic 3, normalizing X_0=1 gives (1,t,t^-1,t^3,t^-5) with t^11=1, and the cubic itself is 5t=2t, not zero. In characteristic 11 the second affine gradient equation forces a,b to be units, and the first then forces s to be a unit. Eliminating with the first, second and fourth gives a=5s^2, b=s^-2, c=5s^-5, and the third gives s^11=4; the fifth is then automatic. This establishes an isomorphism of quotient rings, not just solution-set equality. Euler's identity eliminates the cubic equation from the homogeneous gradient ideal in the chart; equivalently adjoining the cubic to the four affine derivatives recovers the fifth homogeneous derivative. Thus the algebra is k[s]/((s-4)^11) after algebraic closure and the geometric support is P. The rank of the quadratic form is 3, also seen from the one-dimensional tangent to this singular scheme and the affine Hessian at P. Reducibility or nonreducedness would give a positive-dimensional singular locus, and the integral hypersurface satisfies S2 and R1, hence is normal. In centered projective coordinates the equation is X_0 Q(u)+C(u); projection from P has inverse [-C(u):Q(u)u] where Q is nonzero. A direction with Q nonzero contributes one nonvertex point, one with Q=0 and C nonzero contributes none, and Q=C=0 contributes q. A separate finite replay in branches/1cdf91fe-b44d-486d-9f0f-6f8e0fa60d78/check_record3.py confirmed rank 3, 16105 projective representatives and 1464 cubic points over F_11, and the two direction counts 133 and 12 giving the same total. These finite checks are not the proof of geometric uniqueness or of smoothness at other primes.
